newsitem.title: USA: Consumers get added protections in bank reform bill.
newsitem.headline: Consumers get added protections in bank reform bill.

text.p: Consumers would gain substantial new legal protections when buying financial services under amendments added to bank reform legislation by lawmakers on Thursday.

The House Banking Committee, debating proposals to overhaul antiquated U.S. banking laws, approved an amendment to the legislation that would require banks to disclose the risks about various products being offered and sell insured and uninsured products in physically separate locations when possible.
Firms also could not coerce consumers into buying products like mortgage insurance as a condition of receiving a loan or other service.

If the reform bill becomes law, banks, insurance companies and securities firms would be able to combine and offer consumers one-stop shopping for financial services. But consumer groups complained that under the original proposal, large financial companies offering a diverse array of products might mislead or overcharge consumers.

"As consumers deal increasingly with banks that may be part of large-scale diversified financial institutions, they potentially become more vulnerable," said Representative John LaFalce, D.-N.Y., who sponsored the amendment. "We must ensure that consumer interests are protected in this legislation.

After the amendment was adopted, consumer advocates praised the changes but said they still were likely to oppose the bill for other reasons. The groups strongly opposed amendments adopted on Tuesday and Wednesday that would allow banks to own or be owned by nonfinancial, commercial companies.

"The amendments are very important to consumers but the concentration of economic power that is obvious in the mixing of banking and commerce is a huge problem," said Jake Lewis, a banking specialist who works for consumer advocate Ralph Nader.

The committee still has not voted on the entire bill and even if the panel approved the legislation, numerous hurdles remain before it could become law. For more than a decade, congress has been debating bank reform to dismantle the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act, but the proposals have always been blocked by disputes among the major industries involved.
LaFalce toned down some parts of his amendment from an earlier version to get more support from Republicans, but bankers said they were still unhappy with some provision.
Banks would be required to ensure consumers only purchased "suitable" investments, which could expose them to lawsuits from customers who lose money on investments.

The anti-coercion rules were also broadly worded, upsetting some bankers. Banks could not engage "in any practice that would lead a consumer to believe" that an extension of credit was dependent on buying another product.
The amendment would require banks to set up physically separate areas for offering federally insured services, like bank accounts, and uninsured products, like mutual funds.
A newly created National Council of Financial Services would have to conduct a study on whether any additional regulations were needed to protect consumer privacy, the amendment said.
